text:
St. Francis Borgia
Confessor
October 10th

“Francis, fourth Duke of Gandia, was the son of John Borgia and of Joanna of Aragon, grand-daughter of Ferdinand the Catholic. He passed his childhood, in his father’s house, in wonderful innocence and piety; but appeared still more admirable when he showed himself a pattern of Christian virtue and austerity, first at the court of the Emperor, Charles V, and afterwards as viceroy of Catalonia. He was charged to convey the body of the Empress Isabelle to her sepulcher at Granada. Seeing the horrible change in her features, he understood how fleeting are all earthly things, and vowed to renounce everything as soon as possible, and devote himself to the service of the King of kings. From that day forward he made such progress in virtue that, in the midst of overwhelming occupations, his life was a faithful copy of religious perfection, so that he was called the miracle of princes.

On the death of his wife Eleonora de Castro, he entered the Society of Jesus, that he might therein be more hidden, on account of the vow which closes the door to ecclesiastical preferment. Many princes followed him in embracing a severe manner of life; and Charles V himself did not hesitate to acknowledge that his advice and example had led him to abdicate the throne. Francis devoted himself to the exercises of a penitential life, and macerated his body by fasting, iron chains, a rough hair-shirt, long and bloody disciplines, allowing himself very little sleep; while at the same time he spared no effort to conquer himself and to gain souls. His great virtue caused St. Ignatius to appoint him Commissary general for Spain; and soon afterwards, against his will, he was chosen by the whole Society third General of the Order. In this position his prudence and holiness endeared him both to Popes and to temporal rulers. He founded and enlarged many houses of his Order, and introduced the Society into Poland, the islands of the Atlantic, Mexico, and Peru, and sent apostolic men into other regions who spread the Catholic, Roman faith by their preaching, their labors, and their blood.

He had a most lowly opinion of himself, always calling himself the sinner. This humility led him to persistently refuse the Roman purple, which was more than once offered him by the Pope. Filled with contempt for himself and the world, he delighted in sweeping away dirt, begging alms from door to door, and serving the sick in the hospitals. He devoted many hours every day to heavenly contemplation, spending sometimes eight or even ten hours in prayer, and genuflecting in adoration a hundred times in the day. He never omitted saying Mass. While he was offering the divine Victim, or preaching, the heavenly ardor which consumed him betrayed itself by the radiance of his countenance. He knew by a heavenly instinct where the most holy Body of Christ, hidden in the Eucharist, was kept. Saint Pius V appointed Francis companion to Cardinal Alessandrino, in an embassy for uniting the Christian princes against the Turks. Although his strength was almost exhausted, he undertook this journey in obedience; but on the way he happily closed his life, as he had wished, at Rome, in the sixty-second year of his age, and in the year of salvation 1572. By Saint Teresa, who had often sought his advice, he was called a saint, and by Gregory XIII a faithful servant of God. Finally, after many great miracles, he was canonized by Clement X.”

(The Liturgical Year, 1841-1875, Dom Prosper Guéranger)

text:
Brown fat burns more energy in the morning and in the cold, and it barely runs while you sleep. A new preprint finds one mitochondrial protein that responds to the body clock, cold, and dietary fat all at once.

Researchers from the University of Copenhagen, UPenn, and collaborators studied SLC25A34, a mitochondrial transporter that no one had assigned a job to. Mitochondria are the compartments in your cells that burn fuel for energy in the form of ATP, and transporters are the gates that move molecules in and out of them.

A little primer on some of the concepts of the study:

Brown fat is a heat-producing tissue. Its cells run a loop: they build fat in the cytosol, the fluid outside the mitochondria, then burn it inside the mitochondria. Building and burning at the same time looks wasteful. That waste is the point, because it releases energy as heat. In humans, brown fat activity is linked to better metabolic health.

What the study found:

• Cold exposure raised SLC25A34 about 90-fold in mouse brown fat within 24 hours, making it the most enriched tissue for this gene, ahead of the heart

• During sleep, the clock protein REV-ERBα keeps the gene switched off. Waking or cold removes that brake

• A fat-sensing protein called PPARα then switches the gene on, and it responds to the fats released when cells break down stored fat

• A ketogenic diet (93% fat) made it the second most induced gene in the entire brown fat transcriptome. A standard high-fat diet had a much smaller effect

• Silencing the gene in brown fat cells reduced respiration, fat synthesis, and mitochondrial content, and acetyl-CoA levels dropped

Acetyl-CoA is the raw material cells use to build fat, and it also helps signal genes to make more mitochondria.

The proposed mechanism: when cells make acetyl-CoA outside the mitochondria, a leftover molecule called oxaloacetate gets stranded in the cytosol. SLC25A34 appears to carry it back in, which keeps the building and burning loop moving. Without the transporter, oxaloacetate piled up outside and fell inside the mitochondria. Adding acetate, an alternative source of acetyl-CoA, largely rescued the damage.

There is also an early human signal. Across 23 clinical studies, SLC25A34 in subcutaneous fat was linked to lower BMI, waist circumference, triglycerides, and insulin resistance, and to higher HDL. The correlations were small, and no link appeared in belly fat around the organs.

This is a preprint, most of the work is in mice and cultured cells, and direct proof that the protein transports oxaloacetate is still pending. Whether the same circuit matters in human brown fat is unknown.

What this means for longevity and health optimization:

No one has tested whether you can raise SLC25A34 on purpose, so none of this is a protocol. But the findings line up with habits that already have support, and they offer a possible mechanism for why those habits work.

• Cold exposure: Cold was the strongest trigger in the study. It fits with research linking regular cold exposure to more active brown fat, though the best dose for people is still unclear

• Sleep and circadian rhythm: The clock brake that keeps this gene off at night is released around waking. Consistent sleep and wake times, and morning light, may help your brown fat switch on on schedule

• Diet composition: Very high fat intake, as in a ketogenic diet, turned the gene on in mice. That doesn't mean keto boosts brown fat in humans, and a standard high-fat diet had a much smaller effect

• Mitochondrial health: Brown fat declines with age and with obesity. Keeping it active may be one way to preserve mitochondrial capacity in a tissue that burns fat and clears glucose

The larger point is that timing, temperature, and fuel all converge on the same mitochondrial gate.

I love building. Maybe too much. One of the consequences is that I have a ton of projects. My Vercel account has at least 50, probably close to 100. I have Supabase projects running for apps that need databases and auth. I have a SendGrid account for email. Upstash for key-value and rate limits. Supabase Storage and Cloudflare R2 for files. And so on.

And that’s when everything is managed! There are so many services you have to package together just to get something up and running. Doing it from scratch used to mean knowing everything, from provisioning servers to security to databases.

Well, that used to be the case anyway. As we all know (hopefully), AI has changed the game. The threshold of capability keeps going up. People are reverse-engineering AAA games and closed-source software like Photoshop. Of course it’s not perfect, but it doesn’t need to be. It just has to solve your problem. And the gap between what these companies offer and your own vibe-coded solution gets smaller and smaller (for your use case).

I was sick of paying Supabase $25 just to spin up a new database. I was sick of getting nervous as my Vercel bill crept up with more obscure charges for features I had no idea about.

As much as I love these companies, they’re in a tough spot. They raised money in a pre-AI world where healthy SaaS margins were the expectation. Now they face more and more competition, margins are compressed, and they have to keep adding features to justify their prices.

So I decided to take control of my software. I wanted one box with everything I need, from databases and auth to email, running my apps over HTTPS. Basically Supabase + Vercel + Resend/SendGrid.

And I think I did it. I’m really excited about this project. I’m calling it ShipTiffin (because the box is a tiffin… ha ha).

Each box comes with:

-Apps, deployed from GitHub, the CLI or your coding agent
- A database
- Auth
- Email
- Jobs (queues and scheduled crons)
- File storage
- Analytics
- Backups

It’s “bring your own infra.” You bring a Hetzner server, and ShipTiffin configures everything so you can build as many apps as you like on the box (you can probably ship dozens without an issue). Each project gets its own database, KV, email and deployment URLs. It’s ready in about five minutes.

The best part: you’ll never wake up to a crazy bill because of a bot attack or a traffic spike. You pay for your server, plus a flat fee to ShipTiffin if you want it managed. The same setup bought separately runs about $130 a month; on ShipTiffin it’s $19 plus about $10 for the server. And frankly, for most apps that’s more than enough. I even found my apps to be faster than on Vercel, depending on the region.

Why Hetzner? Simply because it has the best price-performance you can get. The egress bandwidth is super generous too (20 TB a month in Europe). You can go crazy with apps and services (a web app here, an agent scheduler there, a database backend) without sweating.

To be clear, I'm not claiming I can match Vercel (yet). Maybe don’t throw your prod site on it for now. But I think it’s a really interesting alternative way to build projects without worrying about all the charges these companies will throw at you as they navigate a moatless future. Once you grow, you can resize the box, scale out to other services, or export your data and move elsewhere.

And it’s open source: https://t.co/tigx0eDnif

Run it yourself on any server for free, or let me run it for you. ShipTiffin is live today too. No waitlist. The first 100 customers pay $12 a month, locked for two years. No VC here, just me and my agent building.

I’m super excited and a little scared, and I’d appreciate any feedback. Please check it out and let me know what you think!

My inability to obtain satisfactory resolution of cybersecurity incidents I attributed to the U.S. Department of State and Meta in 2020, compounded by concerns surrounding FBI threat-messaging narratives amplified through News Corp media outlets during 2020–2021, directly influenced my decision to abandon the consumer cybersecurity and venture capital markets.

The four categories I identified—foreign state-sponsored hackers, terrorism, child exploitation, and phishing or financial fraud—contributed to what I perceived as an increasingly adverse reputational and institutional environment for individuals raising cybersecurity concerns.

Although I had developed Metaseeker's consumer privacy portfolio and recognized its potential venture capital appeal, I concluded that continued participation in the sector would expose me to institutional relationships and professional dynamics from which I sought independence.

Consequently, in late 2022 and throughout 2023, I redirected my entrepreneurial resources toward Skipyo's proposed hedge fund and public equity investment strategies, prioritizing financial autonomy over Metaseeker's potential commercial upside. In retrospect, this represented a material opportunity-cost decision: my assessment of institutional risk took precedence over product-market validation and venture scalability.

In retrospect, my decision to prioritize Skipyo's hedge fund strategy over Metaseeker may have constituted a significant capital allocation miscalculation. Metaseeker offered exposure to an expanding cybersecurity and consumer privacy market, with potential for scalable software economics, venture financing, and relatively capital-efficient product validation.

Skipyo, conversely, required institutional limited-partner commitments, credible investment performance, regulatory infrastructure, and substantial assets under management before achieving comparable economic viability. By seeking independence from the cybersecurity and venture capital ecosystems, I effectively exchanged a potentially scalable product opportunity for a financial services model characterized by higher institutional entry barriers and greater dependence on external capital allocation decisions.

Although the decision reflected my assessment of unresolved cybersecurity concerns and the importance of professional autonomy, the economic trade-off was unfavorable if Metaseeker could have demonstrated sustainable customer acquisition and product-market fit. The central entrepreneurial lesson is that institutional disengagement should be weighed against addressable market opportunity, capital efficiency, execution control, and the preservation of strategic optionality.

Also in retrospect, Accenture's alleged cybersecurity red-teaming posture in 2022 could have provided a potential pathway for positioning Metaseeker within Silicon Valley's venture capital ecosystem, leveraging my consulting experience, proximity to technology investors, and growing market demand for consumer privacy solutions.

However, my unresolved concerns regarding the 2020 cybersecurity incidents I attributed to the State Department and Meta, compounded by what I perceived as the FBI's 2020–2021 threat-messaging posture amplified through News Corp media properties, materially influenced my unwillingness to pursue that opportunity.

I regarded the associated narratives concerning foreign hackers, terrorism, child exploitation, and financial cybercrime as creating reputational and institutional risks incompatible with my entrepreneurial objectives.

Consequently, rather than capitalize on a potentially favorable environment for Metaseeker's development and venture financing, I elected to disengage from the cybersecurity and technology investment ecosystems and prioritize Skipyo's hedge fund strategy.

The resulting opportunity cost was the decision to forgo potential venture-backed commercialization in favor of institutional independence, despite Skipyo's substantially higher limited-partner fundraising and market-entry barriers. This explains how my perception of the institutional environment shaped the decision; it does not establish that Accenture offered a venture financing pathway specifically routed through their SV VC networks however it does establish that a coordinated FBI–News Corp campaign from 2020/2021 and the messaging that the cyber industry frequently introduced prevented my interest in seeking Metaseeker's commercialization.

My decision to prioritize Skipyo's public equity and proposed hedge fund investment strategy in late 2022, rather than continue commercializing Metaseeker, created an unexpected pathway into corporate governance innovation. Through Skipyo's investment activities, I established equity positions in four publicly traded companies at levels I understood to satisfy applicable shareholder proposal eligibility thresholds, creating opportunities to examine shareholder rights, board accountability, corporate disclosures, and investor participation mechanisms.

In 2022, this involvement extended to pursuing Microsoft Board of Directors documentation through legal proceedings in Delaware and Washington State, exposing practical challenges associated with information access, governance transparency, and the exercise of shareholder rights. These experiences revealed what I considered a structural inefficiency in public capital markets: despite widespread equity ownership, shareholders lacked a unified, accessible infrastructure for verified discussion, collective engagement, and informed interaction with corporate issuers.

This observation became the foundation for Zindaca, a Shareholder Governance Platform, conceived to connect verified retail and institutional shareholders, facilitate issuer engagement, and democratize access to governance-related information and education.

By mid-2023, I had translated these experiences into an entrepreneurial proposition and pitched Zindaca to Y Combinator, marking a return to technology entrepreneurship through financial market infrastructure rather than consumer cybersecurity or LPA-side Fund Management to evaluate FinTech Startup options.

The strategic irony was that Skipyo's institutional financing challenges ultimately helped generate a potentially venture-scalable governance technology concept in an adjacent sector after an initial decision to move away from Silicon Valley venture capital created the firsthand market insight underlying Zindaca's formation. The broader lesson is that direct participation in complex institutional markets can reveal infrastructure gaps capable of supporting new technology ventures, even when the original investment strategy encounters barriers to scale.

Between 2020 and 2022, I experienced what I understood to be cybersecurity breaches involving Twitter, alongside unresolved concerns regarding other technology platforms. Having subsequently developed investment experience in Twitter through Skipyo's public equity activities, I was preparing to approach Jack Dorsey's former Twitter leadership and cybersecurity personnel to pursue a discreet, technically grounded review of the reported incidents.

My objective was to establish whether historical security records, internal technical expertise, and relevant personnel could substantiate the incidents and facilitate a resolution without unnecessary public escalation.

However, Elon Musk's October 2022 acquisition of Twitter fundamentally altered the company's leadership and institutional structure. The subsequent large-scale workforce reductions, including reported departures across security and technical functions, created uncertainty regarding the continuity of personnel and institutional knowledge potentially relevant to reviewing historical incidents. Although those organizational changes did not establish that evidence had been lost or that a resolution was impossible, they materially reduced my confidence in pursuing the original engagement strategy.

The transition also introduced a different institutional environment. I viewed Musk's relationships across defense technology, national security, Texas-based political and commercial networks, and mass media as potentially complicating an already sensitive cybersecurity matter. These concerns were amplified by what I perceived as Accenture's cybersecurity red-teaming posture toward my employment in 2022 and my earlier concerns regarding FBI threat-messaging narratives carried by News Corp outlets during 2020–2021. I was particularly apprehensive about potential overlap between Musk's media relationships and organizations whose coverage I had previously regarded as adverse. These were assessments of institutional and reputational risk rather than established evidence that Musk, Accenture, News Corp, or government actors coordinated against me.

From an entrepreneurial standpoint, the distinction was consequential. My original position in consumer privacy was explicitly non-defense-oriented: Metaseeker sought to create commercial value by helping individuals protect personal information, reduce unwanted surveillance exposure, and exercise greater control over their digital lives. I regarded unauthorized access, intrusive surveillance, and espionage as risks to be mitigated, not capabilities to be commercialized. In my assessment, deeper engagement with defense-connected cybersecurity networks risked diluting that market positioning, introducing conflicts between consumer trust and national security-oriented commercial relationships. Combined with the Twitter ownership transition and my unresolved employment-related concerns, this created what I considered an unfavorable risk-adjusted environment for continuing Metaseeker or pursuing a quiet resolution through Twitter's former leadership.

Consequently, in late 2022 and throughout 2023, I pursued what I considered the most aggressive but potentially liberating strategic alternative: repositioning Skipyo toward a hedge fund and institutional public equities investment model. Rather than depend on Silicon Valley venture financing or the Washington–Arlington national security technology ecosystem, I sought to establish an independent investment management business through prospective CFA- and pension-related institutional relationships, limited-partner commitments, and conventional capital markets infrastructure. Had those financing efforts succeeded, Skipyo could potentially have operated with greater strategic autonomy, following a traditional New York-style investment management model governed by applicable securities laws, SEC requirements, fiduciary responsibilities, and institutional investor agreements. The intended outcome was not exemption from oversight, but independence from technology-sector gatekeepers through a legally structured, commercially disciplined financial enterprise.

The resulting trade-off was substantial. The world's first indoor rodeo is traditionally credited to Fort Worth, Texas, March 11–16, 1918, at the North Side Coliseum, now known as Cowtown Coliseum, in the Fort Worth Stockyards.  That building is shown in the accompanying photo. The rodeo was part of the Southwestern Exposition and Fat Stock Show. It featured 12 performances over six days, drew approximately 23,000 spectators, and offered $3,000 in prize money.   As I said, it was the first indoor rodeo.

Or was it?  I just learned that the previous year, in 1917, famed cowgirl Lucille Mulhall organized an indoor competition called Lucille Mulhall's Round-Up in that very same building. More than 50 cowboys and cowgirls competed for prizes in roping, bronc riding, and other events.  Rodeo historian Richard Rattenbury, formerly of the National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum, considers Mulhall's 1917 competition the actual first indoor rodeo, even though Lucile (whose photo I posted yesterday) didn't call it a rodeo.   Nevertheless, from the description, it's clear to me that it WAS a rodeo.

So not only was the first indoor rodeo held in Fort Worth, but it was put on by a woman.  I'm not sure how I didn't know this before now but I'll be danged if that's not the God's honest truth.  15+ years doing Traces of Texas and I'm learning new stuff every day.

Why did the Normans never cross the boarder to Scotland they had the numbers, they crossed the Irish sea.

The Normans actually did cross the border into Scotland on multiple occasions—William the Conqueror himself led a combined army and fleet into Scotland in 1072

. However, they chose not to launch a full-scale conquest and occupation like they did in England. [1, 2]
While they had the numbers, their restraint regarding Scotland—contrasted with their crossing of the Irish Sea—comes down to a mix of geography, economics, and a highly successful strategy of "soft power" colonisation.1. 
The Strategy: Submission over Slaughter

When William the Conqueror marched into Scotland in 1072 to punish King Malcolm III for raiding northern England, he didn't seek to depose him.
 At Abernethy, William used a classic Norman tactic: he forced Malcolm to bow, sign the Treaty of Abernethy, hand over his son as a hostage, and swear fealty to William as his feudal overlord. [1, 2, 3]

For the Normans, a submissive buffer state to the north was vastly preferable to a costly, bloody occupation. 

They achieved their geopolitical goals without losing a single drop of Norman blood in a prolonged war.2. 

High Cost, Low Reward

The Norman military machine relied heavily on heavily armoured cavalry and building stone castles to dominate flat, agriculturally rich landscapes. 

Scotland’s geography—dominated by bogs, dense forests, and the mountainous Highlands—was an absolute nightmare for mounted knights. 

[1, 2]Furthermore, from a purely financial perspective, Scotland was relatively poor.
 It lacked the highly centralised, wealthy Anglo-Saxon tax system that had made England such a lucrative prize. 
To the Normans, a scorched-earth conquest of the Highlands offered almost no economic return on a massive military investment. [1]3. 

The Davidian Revolution: "Conquest" by Invitation

The most fascinating reason the Normans never violently conquered Scotland is that they didn't need to—they were invited in.

In the 12th century, King David I of Scotland (who had grown up in the Anglo-Norman court in England) took the throne.
 He wanted to modernise Scotland, so he voluntarily introduced Norman feudalism, laws, and administrative systems to his kingdom. [1, 2]

David invited prominent Norman barons north and granted them vast Scottish estates in exchange for their military allegiance. 

This "peaceful Norman conquest" was so profound that many of the most famous figures in Scottish history were actually of Norman descent: [1, 2]Robert the Bruce was descended from the Norman knight Robert de Brus.

> A comment period with a predetermined outcome—often referred to as a "constructive predetermination"—violates the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which requires agencies to keep an open mind during notice-and-comment. Courts strike down rules or permits if an agency’s settlement contract effectively binds its regulatory discretion before public input is heard.
>
> The most notable legal context for this scenario involves the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the APA. Landmark cases on this issue highlight the illegality of "rubber-stamping" agreements.
>
> Notable Precedents:
>
> Endangered Species Committee v. Babbitt (9th Cir. 1995): This case is a defining precedent. The court found that when an agency binds itself to a specific outcome in a settlement agreement, any subsequent NEPA review becomes a meaningless formality. The court established that agencies cannot legally "pre-determine" the outcome of a decision before the public comment period or environmental analysis has concluded.
>
> Kern v. United States Bureau of Land Management (9th Cir. 2002): The court reinforced that NEPA compliance must occur before any irretrievable commitment of resources. An agency cannot enter into a settlement agreement that contractually commits it to a specific land-use decision prior to evaluating public comments and environmental impacts.
>
> Sierra Club v. Marsh (1st Cir. 1987): The court ruled that an agency violates NEPA if it structures its administrative process so that the outcome is a foregone conclusion. The court emphasized that public input must be capable of actually influencing agency decision-making, not just justifying a deal already struck.
>
> How Courts Rule
> When an agency signs a settlement agreement that forces a pre-determined outcome, they usually fall into one of two major legal traps:
>
> Bad Faith Predetermination:
> Courts view it as a failure to take a "hard look" at the evidence, rendering the decision arbitrary and capricious under the APA.
>
> End-Run around Public Input: The agency unlawfully skirts the notice-and-comment requirements by promising a specific outcome to a litigating party before public concerns are even aired.
>
> Recourse
>
> If a proposed settlement dictates the final rule or decision before the comment period has officially opened, impacted parties can challenge the action by filing a lawsuit under the APA. They laid track, cut cloth, opened shops, and raised children who spoke English and paid taxes. That was the bargain. America offered the chance. The immigrant did the work.
When did that bargain die?
When Washington decided a humanitarian stamp was a claim on the American paycheck.
When “looking for a better life” replaced a skill, a job, and a refusal to live off strangers.

When resettlement became an industry, and dependency became the product.

The new arrival was no longer asked what he could build. He was enrolled.
October 1 ends that arrangement for full Medicaid. Iowa Health and Human Services was plain about it. Coverage is for citizens, lawful permanent residents, and a narrow list of other groups. Refugees, asylees, Afghan evacuees without a green card, and people here on humanitarian parole no longer qualify unless they have become permanent residents. Iowa is still covering lawfully present children. Emergency care remains. The automatic benefit does not. About 973 people in Iowa lose it. Across the country the number runs into the hundreds of thousands. The advocates are calling it cruel. It is the first honest rule these programs have had in years.
No one is entitled to a free life here. A better life is not issued at the airport. It is built, the way it was built by the people who came before there was a welfare office to receive them. If that sounds hard, it is the same hardness that made the country worth entering. The public-charge standard always said a green card is for those who will not become a burden. We stopped meaning it. These newcomers are about to learn what Americans already know: the dream is not a handout. It is work.

America was built by immigrants who arrived ready to work. It will not be maintained by arrivals who arrived ready to enroll.

Brigitte Gabriel

Trump announced a deal with Putin to supply up to 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel to American and global markets, promising rapidly falling prices.

Russia's refining capacity is already under sustained pressure from Ukraine's long-range strike campaign.

Trump's own announcement acknowledges the vulnerability: the final 3 million tons depend on the condition of Russia's refineries.

Read that again.

The White House is promising American consumers cheaper diesel based partly on industrial capacity that Russia cannot guarantee.

And Moscow faces a dilemma.

→ Export diesel to fulfill Trump's agreement and earn revenue, potentially worsening domestic shortages.

→ Prioritize domestic consumption and risk failing to deliver the promised volumes.

→ Redirect existing exports and claim a supply victory without meaningfully increasing global availability.

Ukraine doesn't need to change its military objectives for this contradiction to become consequential. Its existing campaign against Russia's war economy already intersects with the agreement's central vulnerability.

But Kyiv has another weapon: transparency.

Demand verification of every shipment, every additional barrel, every payment, and every dollar flowing into Moscow's war economy.

Because redirecting Russian diesel is not the same as creating new global supply.

And lifting restrictions on Russian energy revenues while Moscow continues invading Ukraine raises a question Washington cannot escape:

Is America lowering diesel prices—or financing the country destroying Ukraine?

The agreement has three tests: Can Russia produce it? Can Russia deliver it? And will American consumers actually benefit?

Until those questions are answered, Trump has announced a promise, not an economic victory.

Her mother bought her a pair of figure skates, hoping she would take up something more ladylike.

She was born Marcenia Lyle Stone in 1921 and the family moved to the Rondo neighborhood of St. Paul when she was ten. The boys on the block called her Tomboy.

Softball was offered to her and she turned it down. She said it was not fast enough.

A priest at her church noticed her arm and got her onto the parish team, but the coach there had no interest in teaching a girl anything. So she went and got the rulebooks and taught herself.

Then she started showing up at the baseball school run by Gabby Street, who managed the St. Paul Saints.

She kept showing up. Here is how Street described it.

"I just couldn't get rid of her until I gave her a chance."

At 16 she was playing weekends for the barnstorming Twin City Colored Giants for two or three dollars a game. She dropped out of high school to keep playing.

In 1943 she moved to San Francisco and started calling herself Toni. She played for a San Francisco American Legion team, and to get under the age limit she knocked ten years off, telling them she was 17 when she was 27.

Then the San Francisco Sea Lions. Then four seasons with the New Orleans Creoles.

In 1953 the Indianapolis Clowns signed her to play second base.

That was Hank Aaron's position. Aaron had just left the Clowns for the Milwaukee Braves, and Toni Stone took the job he vacated. She was the first woman to play as a regular on a big league professional baseball team.

The owner wanted her in a skirt, for the gate. She refused and wore the uniform, with a foam rubber chest protector under it.

She played 50 games and hit .243.

Here is what that year was actually like.

Her own manager said she had better stick to knitting and home cooking. Teammates told her to go home and fix her husband some biscuits. Most of the men on her own team would not speak to her. She was barred from the clubhouse and dressed in the umpires' room.

Runners went in spikes up. She used to show people the scars.

In 1954 her contract was sold to the Kansas City Monarchs, where she sat. She described that season in three words.

"It was hell."

She retired after it, moved to Oakland, became a nurse, and spent decades caring for her husband, who lived to 103.

She told people the rest of her life that she once got a base hit off Satchel Paige. Researchers have never been able to confirm it. They have never been able to disprove it either.

Toni Stone died in 1996 at 75 years old. She is not in the Baseball Hall of Fame. She has a plaque in an exhibit there and a ballfield in St. Paul and a day named after her.

The Negro League Baseball Players Association put it this way. One of the best players you have never heard of.

She never did learn to skate.

The New York Times
Zohran Mamdani’s Moral Obscenity
By Bret Stephens - Opinion Columnist
Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, set off a firestorm of criticism Wednesday morning with a social media post ostensibly intended to commemorate the Oct. 7, 2023, massacre of Israelis.  It devoted a brief paragraph to condemning Hamas and commiserating with its victims.  The rest was a much longer denunciation of Israel’s “ongoing genocide in Gaza,” a “world in which occupation and apartheid continue” and a situation in which “our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment.”
In response, Ammiel Hirsch, the president of the New York Board of Rabbis, said the statement was “so offensive to so many Jews that it is hard to describe how offensive it is.”  In fact, it’s a moral obscenity.  Let me count the ways.
It is obscene in the same way it would have been obscene if the mayor had commemorated the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11 last month with a perfunctory nod to the victims of the day, followed by a much longer denunciation of U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East.  What happened on both Sept. 11 and Oct. 7 was undiluted evil, each an unprovoked visit of deliberate and maximalist violence on people who had done nothing to invite that violence other than being at the
wrong place at the wrong time.
It is obscene because many of the Jews murdered on Oct. 7, living in kibbutzim with conspicuously left-leaning politics, had been at the forefront of the peace movement, volunteering, for example, to drive sick Palestinians for treatment at nearby Israeli hospitals.  Hamas wasn’t just killing and terrorizing the innocent; it was eliminating the good.
It is obscene because Hamas didn’t just kill its victims in pursuit of a strategic objective.  It tormented and slaughtered them like an army of serial killers who delight in the suffering of their victims.  Corpses of Israeli women were described by one coroner as “shot in the crotch, intimate parts, vagina, or were shot in the breast.”  Others appeared to have been raped so violently that their pelvises were broken.  Parents were killed in front of their children; children were murdered in their beds. A fieldworker was beheaded with a garden hoe.  I know this because Hamas filmed itself doing this and I forced myself to watch the film.  I know because that same month, I visited the bedrooms where the kids had been murdered, their mattresses still soaked in blood.
It is obscene because, whatever else you may think of the war in Gaza, on the eve of Oct. 7 the border of Israel and Gaza was governed by a cease-fire.  It was Hamas that chose to kick off the violence, just as the Japanese did in 1941 with the attack on Pearl Harbor.  Whether in fistfights between people or wars between states, whoever throws the first punch forfeits the right to throw the last.
It is obscene because Mamdani is being misleading when he speaks as if his prime objection to Israel is what it did after Oct. 7.   In fact, the mayor has been an anti-Israel zealot at least since his college days, when, as a leader of Students for Justice in Palestine, he broke off collaboration with the left-leaning Jewish group J Street, which advocates a Palestinian state, because it also recognizes the rights of a Jewish state.  He’s written a rap professing “love” for five men convicted  in a U.S. court of funneling money to Hamas.  The day after Oct. 7, he issued a brief statement that said nothing about Hamas but immediately denounced Israel. Put simply, this is a mayor who first condemned Israel as guilty and then went about collecting evidence.
It is obscene because, however much the genocide allegation against Israel is mindlessly repeated by people too lazy or prejudiced to understand the difference between war and genocide, that allegation is as false as it is sinister.  False, because genocide is about killing whole classes of people for who they are rather than for what they did — and if Israel wanted to kill Palestinians as Palestinians it never would have bothered mobilizing hundreds of thousands of its own soldiers for the war, and losing hundreds in high-intensity urban warfare.  Sinister, because the political purpose of the genocide allegation is to trivialize, if not erase, the attacks of Oct. 7 by making them seem minor in comparison to the Palestinian casualties that tragically, but all-but inevitably, followed.
It is obscene because Hamas’s intentions toward Israel really are genocidal.  Its leaders have often and publicly vowed
to perpetrate future Oct. 7s.  Had the group not been stopped by force that day, there’s no reason to think it wouldn’t have kept up its orgy of slaughter on its way to Tel Aviv and other Israeli cities.  Yet one searches in vain for anything from the mayor except perfunctory, pro forma condemnations of Hamas.
It is obscene because there’s an even more wretched purpose to the genocide charge against Israel, which long predates the recent war in Gaza.  It is a specimen of Holocaust erasure: not the dumb kind, which seeks to deny Nazi Germany’s murder of six million Jews, but a more sophisticated version that accuses living Jews of genocide as a way of ending the historical Jewish claim to a long and ongoing history of persecution and near-annihilation that accounts for its need for a sovereign state capable of defending its people.
Finally, it is obscene because Mamdani is the mayor for about one million Jewish New Yorkers, many with close relatives in Israel, who deserve better on a day of grief than to be offered the equivalent of an “All Lives Matter” homily.  This is yet another of the double standards through which modern-day Jew hatred manifests itself:  Whenever antisemitism is mentioned in progressive circles, it is inevitably accompanied by nods about Islamophobia or other bigotries.
It would be better to have a mayor who, if only on Oct. 7, can say:
Jewish Lives Matter.
Israeli Lives Matter.
Full stop.

text:
Significance of October 9 in Biblical History
October 9 is marked in Scripture by the Israelites’ observance of the Festival of Shelters (Sukkot) and by the commemoration of Old Testament patriarchs, especially Abraham, in Christian tradition.
Biblical Event — The Festival of Shelters
According to Nehemiah 8:13–10:39, on October 9 the leaders of the Israelite community, along with priests and Levites, met with Ezra the scribe to study the Law more closely 📷Bible Gateway. They discovered that the Lord had commanded through Moses that the Israelites live in temporary shelters during the festival in that month. The people gathered branches from olive, myrtle, palm, and other trees to build shelters on their roofs, courtyards, and even in the Temple grounds. This marked the first time since the days of Joshua that the exiles celebrated the festival in this manner, filled with joy and obedience to God’s command 📷Bible Gateway.
The day also set the stage for the communal reading of the Law and the people’s confession of sins, underscoring themes of faithful obedience, communal worship, and remembrance of God’s covenant.
Christian Commemoration — St. Abraham the Patriarch
In Eastern Christian tradition, October 9 is also the feast day of St. Abraham the Patriarch, honored as “the Father of All Believers” 📷New Liturgical Movement. Abraham is central to biblical salvation history, called the “father of faith” in the New Testament, and is remembered for his willingness to offer his son Isaac and for his role in establishing covenantal faith. His commemoration highlights the foundational role of the Old Testament patriarchs in Christian liturgy and theology.
Historical and Theological Significance
Biblical obedience and joy: The October 9 event in Nehemiah shows the importance of restoring God’s commands and celebrating them with joy.
Covenantal memory: The festival recalls Israel’s covenant with God, reinforcing the continuity between the Old and New Testaments.
Martyrdom and witness: In Christian history, October 9 also marks the martyrdom of Denis of Paris in 250 AD, whose steadfastness in witness to Christ inspired later generations 📷Bible Hub.
In summary, October 9 in biblical history is significant for the Israelites’ joyful observance of the Festival of Shelters as recorded in Nehemiah, and in Christian tradition for the commemoration of St. Abraham, both underscoring themes of covenant faithfulness, obedience, and the enduring witness of the faithful.

text:
Ben Johnson was earning just $30 a month as a cowboy on an Oklahoma ranch when an unexpected opportunity changed his life. In 1940, at age 22, he agreed to deliver a dozen horses to Arizona for $300—ten months of wages for a single trip. Hollywood producer Howard Hughes noticed his extraordinary ability with horses and offered him a job as a wrangler. For seven years, Johnson worked behind the scenes, handling horses and performing dangerous stunts for stars like John Wayne, Gary Cooper, and James Stewart. Everything changed in 1948 when Johnson chased down a runaway wagon carrying three men during the filming of Fort Apache. Director John Ford witnessed the incredible feat and offered him a contract worth $5,000 a week. Johnson transitioned from stuntman to actor, appearing in Western classics such as She Wore a Yellow Ribbon, Rio Grande, and Wagon Master.
But Hollywood fame wasn't his greatest ambition. Raised by a father who was a world-champion roper, Johnson felt a deep calling to the rodeo arena. In 1953, he walked away from acting for an entire year to pursue that dream. He competed in major rodeos across the country and ultimately became the World Champion Team Roper. The victory came at a price: after a year of travel and competition expenses, he had virtually no money left. Yet he had achieved something deeply personal. Johnson eventually returned to Hollywood, continuing to compete in rodeos and using his success to support charitable events. In 1971, he accepted a role in The Last Picture Show after John Ford persuaded him to reconsider the script. His portrayal of Sam the Lion earned widespread acclaim, and in 1972, he won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. During his acceptance speech, he declared that his rodeo championship belt meant more to him than the Oscar, earning a standing ovation.
Johnson continued acting for decades, appearing in more than 300 productions while remaining devoted to his ranching and rodeo roots. He helped organize celebrity rodeos that raised millions for children's hospitals and received numerous honors, including induction into the ProRodeo Hall of Fame and a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. He died of a heart attack in 1996 at the age of 77, leaving behind an extraordinary legacy. Ben Johnson achieved what few people could even imagine: he became both an Academy Award-winning actor and a world rodeo champion, bridging two vastly different worlds without abandoning either. He may have called himself a cowboy who got lucky, but luck alone doesn't tame runaway horses, win world championships, or deliver an Oscar-winning performance. His life was proof that success means little if you lose touch with who you are—and that the greatest achievement is reaching the top without forgetting where you started.

Villas at Trouville

卡耶博特《特鲁维尔别墅》：19世纪法国现代视角

《特鲁维尔别墅》创作于1884年，是法国画家居斯塔夫·卡耶博特在其绘画生涯中极具代表性的一件作品。画布尺寸为66 x 81.3厘米，作者以油画技法细腻展现了法国诺曼底海岸特鲁维尔的小镇景致。这幅作品描绘了从悬崖上俯瞰的蓝绿色海面，映衬着斑驳的云层，前景中是宁静而富有私密感的砖砌别墅，构成了一幅典型的19世纪海滨度假风光。

作品与身份认同

居斯塔夫·卡耶博特不仅是印象派画家，也是法国上层社会的成员和著名的帆船竞技者。这幅画是他在1880年代早期夏季多次前往诺曼底海岸期间创作的。凭借对建筑的关注和光线的精准捕捉，卡耶博特展现了当时新兴的私人海滨别墅文化，这是一种崭新的生活方式象征，也反映了19世纪中产阶级对自然和现代生活的向往。

材质与构造

此画为油画布作品，尺寸适中，更适合于细节描绘。卡耶博特利用厚涂与细腻笔触相结合的技法，表现海面的波光粼粼以及天空层次分明的云朵。砖砌别墅的纹理通过富有层次的色彩堆叠而呈现真实感，同时不失画面的整体和谐。

装饰与绘画细节

画作中，海天一线被云影点缀，海色呈现蓝绿色调，表现出夏日阳光与海水的互动。屋顶和建筑物的红砖与绿植形成鲜明对比。细致入微的笔触，使得建筑物的阴影、光照变化非常生动。整体色彩虽真实，却带有印象派柔和光感的特征，既写实又带有诗意。

题款、印记和文献证据

画作右下角有签名，尽管署名为“G. Caillebotte”但根据玛丽·贝霍特的研究，这签名由卡耶博特死后由其兄弟马尔蒂亚尔代签，反映作品在流传过程中的身份确认和保存状态。作品历经多位收藏家和画廊，包括巴黎的保罗·雨果、纽约的亚历山大·塔尔诺波尔等，且多次参与展览和拍卖，文献记录中准确标明其题材与创作年代，与卡耶博特诺曼底时期活动相对应。

观赏提示

观察该画时，应重点关注海天交汇处的光影处理，以及别墅红砖与自然环境的色彩协调。注意建筑细节的笔触和颜色变化，这体现了卡耶博特对现代生活细节的独到洞察。签名的存在及其特殊性也值得研究者注目，作为作品鉴定和艺术史资料的重要部分。整体来看，这幅画不仅是风景写实，更展现了19世纪法国社会新兴阶层的文化身份和对自然美景的现代诠释。

综上，《特鲁维尔别墅》是卡耶博特艺术生涯的重要组成部分，也是19世纪法国海滨休闲生活的精彩记录。它通过精湛的技法和温婉的色彩引导观者进入那个时代的风貌与精神世界。

Gustave Caillebotte's "Villas at Trouville": A Window into 19th-Century French Coastal Life

Created in 1884, "Villas at Trouville" stands as a quintessential work by French artist Gustave Caillebotte, a painter known for his distinct approach within the Impressionist milieu and his ties to the French bourgeoisie. This oil on canvas, measuring 66 by 81.3 centimeters, offers a carefully observed view of the Normandy coast’s resort town, Trouville, capturing a moment of serene coastal life along the northern shores of France.

Context and Identity

Caillebotte was not only a painter but also an accomplished sailor and a nuanced observer of modern life and architecture. This work belongs to the early 1880s summers when he spent considerable time along the Normandy coast engaging in painting as well as sailing competitions. Here, Caillebotte explores the intersection of natural beauty and human habitation through the depiction of private seaside villas—brick-built homes providing owners a quiet retreat just beyond the town center.

Materiality and Construction

Executed in oil on canvas, the painting’s medium allows for rich textural contrasts and subtle gradations of color. The artist combines thick and deft brushwork to render both the shimmering surface of the blue-green sea and the cloudy sky overhead, creating a dynamic interplay of light and atmosphere. Architectural details are carefully delineated, highlighted by layered pigments that evoke the tactile quality of brick and roof tiles, integrating the man-made with the natural environment.

Decorative and Pictorial Elements

The composition features a panoramic seascape dominated by an expansive horizon under a cloud-dappled sky. The palette includes cool blues and greens contrasted with warm brick reds and muted earth tones of the villas and foliage. The luminous quality characteristic of Impressionism softens the realism, infusing the scene with a poetic sense of tranquility. The painting’s brushwork invites close inspection, revealing nuanced shifts in light that suggest the time of day and weather conditions.

Inscriptions, Signatures, and Documentary Records

The painting is signed in the lower right corner with “G. Caillebotte.” However, scholarly research, notably by Marie Berhaut, indicates this signature was added posthumously by Caillebotte’s brother, Martial. This detail underscores the painting’s provenance complexity and highlights its circulation through various prominent collections and galleries. It has passed through hands in Paris and New York, featured in exhibitions as early as 1894, and is documented in several art historical records, confirming its creation date and situating it within Caillebotte’s active period on the Normandy coast.

Points for Viewers

Viewers should pay particular attention to the transitional zone between sea and sky, where the artist’s handling of light creates a subtle yet compelling atmospheric effect. The interplay between the vividness of the brick villas and the more subdued natural elements invites reflection on the themes of leisure, domesticity, and the encroachment of modern life on the coastal landscape. Additionally, the unique nature of the signature serves as a reminder of the artwork’s post-creation history and its journey through various custodians.

Conclusion

"Villas at Trouville" is not merely a landscape painting but a document of social and cultural identity in late 19th-century France. Through its meticulous execution and layered subjects, it reveals Gustave Caillebotte’s deep engagement with modernity, leisure, and place. The painting thus provides a vivid snapshot of a specific time and locale, presented through the eyes of a distinctive artist balancing realism and impressionistic nuance.

John Kiriakou spent 15 years working in the shadows as a CIA officer. Today, at 62, he's walking the runway at New York Fashion Week, racking up millions of views across social media and becoming an unlikely Gen Z internet sensation.

His videos regularly attract millions of views, and his audience of hundreds of thousands of followers has transformed the former intelligence officer into an unexpected voice for a generation that was too young to remember the events that once defined his life.

"I never thought that I would be this figurehead for thousands and thousands of young men between 15 and 35," Kiriakou told Fox News Digital.

That newfound popularity has opened doors he never imagined, including one into the fashion world. Kiriakou is the first to admit he has never considered himself fashionable. During the interview, he joked that the black T-shirt he was wearing cost about $12 and said he only occasionally flipped through GQ to see what men were wearing. Yet in September, he found himself walking the runway for designer Elena Velez at New York Fashion Week — an unexpected appearance for a man better known for the CIA, national security and exposing the agency's interrogation program.

HOUSE GOP BILL MOVES TO CLOSE WHISTLEBLOWER GAPS EXPOSED BY MINNESOTA MEDICAID FRAUD SCANDAL

"I'm 62 years old. When in life am I ever going to get the chance to be on the catwalk at New York Fashion Week?" he said.

Velez, whose runway shows are known for avant-garde fashion and unconventional casting, reached out after hearing Kiriakou's appearances on several podcasts. But the runway is only one chapter in what has become an unlikely second act.

His online popularity accelerated after appearing on Steven Bartlett's "The Diary of a CEO" podcast. Clips from the interview spread rapidly across social media, introducing millions of younger viewers to stories from his years inside the CIA.

For many members of Gen Z, Kiriakou represents a world they never experienced firsthand. He joined the CIA in 1990, serving as both an analyst and counterterrorism officer before leaving the agency in 2004. His online reach now extends well beyond short-form videos. Kiriakou also connects directly with supporters through Cameo, where users can purchase personalized video messages.

Long before he became an internet personality, Kiriakou was at the center of one of the most contentious national security controversies of the post-9/11 era. In 2007, he publicly discussed the CIA's use of waterboarding during the war on terror. He later pleaded guilty to one count of intentionally disclosing information identifying a covert CIA officer and was sentenced to 30 months in federal prison.

CIA WHISTLEBLOWER CLAIMS OBAMA-ERA ESPIONAGE CHARGES AGAINST HIM WERE A TEST RUN FOR TARGETING TRUMP

Many of the young people who now follow him, however, know him first through viral videos rather than the headlines that once defined his career. Most were born after the September 11 attacks and did not experience those events as they unfolded. Kiriakou believes that generational distance is part of what draws Gen Z to his story.

"There is a special place in my heart for Gen Z," he said. "It's because of Gen Z that I’ve been able to turn my life around and to do things that I had, for the last 62 years, never thought I could do."

Kiriakou believes his growing popularity reflects something larger than internet algorithms. He said many young Americans are increasingly skeptical of traditional politics and are searching for voices they view as more authentic.

"Gen Z has the largest number of political independents of any generation," Kiriakou said. "They don't like the Democrats. They don’t like the Republicans because they feel like they’re being lied to."

Kiriakou, who described himself as an "equal opportunity hater," said he believes frustration with both parties has made younger audiences more willing to listen to voices outside the political establishment.

"I think that's why I’m popular with Gen Z — because I’m seen as somebody who’s telling them the truth," he said.

He argues that his appeal isn't rooted in perfection, but in transparency. Rather than trying to present himself as flawless, Kiriakou said he speaks openly about government, politics and his own personal mistakes.

"I have literally nothing to lose," he said. "I have nothing to gain by lying."

That willingness to speak candidly, he said, has allowed him to build an audience that stretches across the political spectrum. Despite his criticism of modern politics, Kiriakou remains optimistic about the next generation.

"I think that these are real leaders in waiting," he said. "I think they're the ones who are going to save the country."

His confidence in Gen Z is shaped in part by his own improbable second act. The life Kiriakou leads today bears little resemblance to the one he expected after leaving the CIA. In addition to hosting a podcast, he has advised a royal family in the Persian Gulf and is set to appear in an upcoming movie.

"I never thought that I would walk in New York Fashion Week, that I'd be an advisor to a royal family in the Persian Gulf, that I’d have my own podcast," he said. "I never thought that I’d act in a Hollywood movie."

FORMER CIA AGENT JOHN KIRIAKOU REVEALS HOW SEX PLAYS A MAJOR ROLE IN ESPIONAGE AND SPYING

Those experiences have reinforced a lesson he now tries to pass along to younger people: don't be afraid to pursue opportunities that fall outside the life you originally envisioned.

"One of the things that I've learned, especially this year since February, is to embrace everything life has to offer," Kiriakou said.

For young people uncertain about what comes next, he said the answer is often simpler than they think.

"You just have to grab it," he said. "Grab it and do it. And have fun and enjoy yourself."

Kiriakou's online following has also given him a new audience for issues he believes will shape the future, including artificial intelligence and national security. During his interview with Fox News Digital, he warned that AI is advancing faster than governments are prepared to manage. "This is the new frontier, AI," Kiriakou said. "It’s developing so quickly."

TRUMP LAUNCHING 'SUPER INTELLIGENCE FORCE' TO ENSURE AMERICAN DOMINANCE

From his perspective, the technology presents two major risks. One is the possibility that artificial intelligence eventually becomes difficult for humans to control. The other is the growing ability of foreign adversaries to weaponize AI against the United States.

"There are two things to worry about here," he said. "One is that AI goes out of control, but two, it’s that our enemies use AI against us."

Kiriakou said the United States has not kept pace with those emerging threats.

"We’re not prepared. No, we’re not," he said.

He pointed to one example that concerns him most: the impact AI could have on undercover intelligence operations. As facial recognition and biometric technology continue to improve, he questioned whether intelligence officers operating under aliases will be able to remain anonymous.

"How in the world do undercover CIA officers or undercover intelligence officers from any country cross borders now or go through airports in an alias, in disguise?"

Questions surrounding national security have also remained central to Kiriakou's own legal battle. He is seeking a presidential pardon related to his conviction for disclosing classified information.

His message to President Donald Trump:

"Barack Obama, Eric Holder and John Brennan ruined my life, and Donald Trump is the only person who can give it back to me," Kiriakou said.

Kiriakou said what happened to him is part of a broader debate over government secrecy, whistleblowers and public accountability, issues he said also influence his views on artificial intelligence and modern surveillance.

AI voice scam traps mom in 5-hour kidnapping nightmare https://t.co/zGGLDvwT7f

I want you to think about the voice of someone you love. You know how that person sounds when they're laughing, and you also know the voice you would hear if they were terrified. So what would you do if your phone rang, and you heard that voice begging you for help? That's what happened to Deborah Del Mastro.

I recently sat down with Deborah on "The CyberGuy Report" podcast to hear her tell this story in her own words. Even after everything she has been through, you can hear how deeply the experience still affects her. Months after the scam, she also told a U.S. Senate committee that she remained "completely traumatized."

The California mother and Navy veteran was having breakfast with her husband when a local number appeared on her phone. The man on the other end claimed a Mexican drug cartel had taken her 37-year-old daughter Sarah. Then Deborah heard the voice that made the threat feel terrifyingly real. "It's my daughter's voice," she told me. "And she's having a panic attack."

For the next five and a half hours, the caller threatened Deborah and her family, sent her and her husband from place to place and demanded thousands of dollars. What Deborah didn't know was that the story unfolding on the phone was very different from what was actually happening to Sarah.

Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.

See the classes and register at https://t.co/x1SwswUebZ

THE FAMILY GROUP CHAT IS A GOLDMINE FOR SCAMMERS

The phone call that changed everything

The call started strangely enough. "I get a local phone call, my area code," Deborah told me. When she answered, the man asked, "Who is this?" Deborah turned the question back on him, and he replied that he was "someone you need to talk to."

Then he asked whether Deborah's daughter was prone to panic attacks. That question immediately got her attention. Deborah could hear commotion in the background before the caller put someone else on the line. She heard Sarah. The voice was crying and struggling to breathe. "I'm so sorry, Mom. I'm so scared," Deborah remembers hearing. "It was exactly her voice," she told me.

There was another reason Deborah believed she was hearing her daughter. Sarah had recently gone through a breakup, and Deborah had heard her daughter sobbing like that only days earlier. The sound on the phone matched something painfully familiar, which made the call even more convincing.

Then came the threat of a Mexican drug cartel

The man told Deborah that Sarah had witnessed something she was never supposed to see in a parking lot. He claimed ties to a Mexican drug cartel and said Sarah had her phone out when she saw what happened. According to Deborah, his boss had ordered him to take her.

Then he told Deborah what they wanted. "They were going to sell her for $20,000 unless I could come up with the money," Deborah told me. The threat became even darker. She said the caller repeatedly talked about selling Sarah and suggested she could "pay her way in other ways," leaving Deborah terrified that the criminals could sexually traffic her daughter. At that point, she believed violent criminals had Sarah.

The scammer made sure Deborah stayed on the phone

One of his first instructions was to bring a phone charger. "He tells me that I better charge my phone or bring a phone charger because if my phone dies before we're finished, I'll never see her again," Deborah recalled. That told me a lot about how carefully this scam was run. The caller needed control. He demanded that Deborah keep the phone connected so he could hear what was happening around her. He wanted to know when she moved, what she was doing and who she was talking to.

At one point, Deborah muted the call so she could speak privately with her husband. The caller noticed and began screaming. He warned her against trying "funny business." Deborah told me, "He wants to keep my phone open right here so he can hear everything." That control continued for five and a half hours.

YOUR FAMILY COULD BE ONE PHONE CALL FROM A BANK SCAM

'Bargaining with the devil'

The caller initially wanted $20,000. Deborah didn't have it. "We just don't have that," she remembers telling him. So she started negotiating for what she believed was her daughter's life. "Now I'm bargaining with the devil," she told me. Deborah said she had roughly $2,000 in savings. The caller instructed her to go to a nearby Walmart and use MoneyGram to wire money to Mexico. She went, keeping the phone where he could hear everything happening around her.

The man warned that people were watching her in the parking lot and claimed undercover police officers were nearby. He also gave Deborah a story to use if anyone questioned the transfer. The caller told her to say she was helping a relative with medical expenses. "Be discreet," she remembers him telling her. That detail bothers me because scammers often go beyond demanding money. They prepare victims to get around the very people who might recognize that something is wrong.

Nobody stopped her

Deborah moved from location to location sending money. When I asked whether anyone challenged her or asked whether she was OK, her answer was immediate. "No. No. Not at all." By then, the scammer had already given her a cover story. He had also spent hours convincing Deborah that talking to someone could get Sarah killed.

In the end, Deborah sent $5,400 through four separate transactions using MoneyGram and Western Union. She said the transfers took all the accessible money she and her husband had. Later, she put it to me another way: "We were held hostage for 5.5 hours." Deborah and her husband could physically move, but emotionally, the caller had them exactly where he wanted them.

Deborah heard Sarah a second time

Several hours into the call, Deborah kept asking to speak with her daughter again. Eventually, the caller agreed, but even that conversation came with instructions. He told Deborah exactly what she could say: "This nightmare is nearly over. We're going to come get you as soon as we can."

Then Sarah's voice responded. "I'm so sorry, Mom. I love you." I asked Deborah again whether it really sounded like her daughter. "It was her voice," she said. "It was absolutely her voice."

Immediately afterward, another man came onto the phone. Deborah described him as an "enforcer" whose threats sounded even harsher. Soon, the scammers demanded more money.

A mother was already thinking about her daughter's life afterward

There's something Deborah later said that gives you an idea of where her mind had gone during those hours. While her husband drove and the caller listened over the phone, Deborah spent much of the trip sitting silently. Instead of wondering whether this could be a scam, her mind went to Sarah and whether she would survive it.

Deborah was already trying to figure out how her daughter would get through life after an experience like this. Paying the ransom was only part of what was running through her mind. She believed something terrible had already happened to her child and started thinking about how she would help Sarah recover afterward. That shows you how completely real this had become to her.

The caller finally says Sarah has been released

Eventually, the man told Deborah the ordeal was over. He claimed they had released Sarah outside a Walmart where Deborah and her husband were waiting. "Go get her," Deborah remembers him saying. Then he hung up.

Deborah could see the front entrance, so she got out of the car and looked for her daughter. Sarah wasn't there. For a moment, Deborah thought the criminals still had her even after taking every dollar she could reach. She frantically looked around before finally calling Sarah herself. Her daughter answered. "Hi, Mom. What's going on?" Sarah was at work.

'I'd never been so relieved to be scammed in my life'

For more than five hours, Deborah believed people were holding her daughter and might kill her or sell her. Then Sarah simply answered her phone from work. "I'd never been so relieved to be scammed in my life," Deborah told me.

She believes she screamed in the parking lot before the tears came. Deborah told Sarah she loved her, and after work, Sarah came to her parents' home. Her mother hugged her and sobbed. The family then went to the local police department to report what had happened. Losing the money hurt, but Sarah was alive.

Sarah immediately suspected an AI voice clone

When Deborah explained what had happened, Sarah had an immediate reaction. "Mom, that was probably an AI clone of my voice," Deborah remembers her saying. Both of Deborah's adult children work in IT, so they already knew this kind of technology existed. Deborah didn't. "I didn't know," she recalls.

Deborah firmly believes she heard an artificial intelligence-generated version of Sarah's voice. We do know the technology exists, and federal authorities have warned about criminals using it. The FTC says scammers can take a short clip of someone's real voice, including audio posted online, and use voice-cloning technology to make a call sound like that person.

How virtual kidnapping scams work

The underlying scam has been around much longer than today's AI tools. The FBI calls it "virtual kidnapping." Criminals claim they have taken someone you love even though no kidnapping occurred.

One classic warning sign closely matches Deborah's experience. The FBI says virtual kidnappers often work hard to keep victims on the phone so they can't check where their loved one actually is. The agency has also warned about ransom demands involving wire transfers to Mexico.

More recently, the FBI warned that criminals are using altered media in virtual kidnapping schemes. AI can make an old scam much more convincing. Deborah put it perfectly: "It is an old scam with new technology."

She's a Navy veteran who usually runs toward a crisis

One reaction Deborah still encounters is the question some people ask after a scam: Why didn't you hang up? Why didn't you know? Why didn't you tell someone? She understands those questions, but she also knows what was happening inside that call.

As a Navy veteran, Deborah describes herself as someone who stays calm in a crisis. "I always say I am the person that runs to the fire, not away from it." Yet the voice on the phone convinced her completely that Sarah was in danger.

That's something I want people to remember before judging anyone who falls for one of these calls. You can know about scams and handle pressure well. Then someone puts the terrified voice of your child in your ear. Criminals understand exactly what kind of emotional reaction they're trying to trigger.

The financial damage hit hard too

The $5,400 represented every readily available dollar Deborah and her husband could access. She says they are seniors living on Social Security along with income from other work, so the loss hit them hard. The following morning, Deborah went to Facebook and told her community what had happened. She also warned that criminals now had "high-tech capability."

Friends began sending money, but Deborah initially resisted because she didn't want to profit from what happened. Eventually, they convinced her to create a fundraiser on GoFundMe limited to replacing what the couple had lost. Her community raised the money back. That support couldn't erase the five-and-a-half-hour ordeal, but it meant a great deal to Deborah. Her community had shown up for her before, and they showed up again.

7 ways to protect your family from an AI voice kidnapping scam

You don't have to become an expert at detecting synthetic audio. In fact, I wouldn't build your family's defense around your ability to recognize a fake voice. A better approach is to decide now how your family will verify an emergency.

1) Call your loved one yourself

If someone claims your child, spouse or another relative has been kidnapped or injured, contact that person directly at the number you already have saved. If they don't answer, try someone who should know where they are. The FTC specifically recommends verifying the story through a phone number you know belongs to your loved one.

2) Create a private family safe word

Choose a word or phrase that someone couldn't easily discover through social media. The FBI recommends establishing a family code word for situations like virtual kidnapping scams.

Deborah also recommends a safe word now, although her experience shows why you need more than one way to verify an emergency. "There was no way I could have done any of that in this particular situation," she told me. The caller controlled when she could speak with Sarah, so don't make a safe word your family's only verification method.

3) Have another way to verify someone's location

After the scam, Deborah and Sarah began using a location-sharing app so each could see where the other was. Apple and Google also offer built-in location-sharing options. If you want to set this up on your phone, see our guide on how to share your whereabouts in any situation using your cell phone.

Location sharing comes with its own privacy considerations, so only share your location with people you trust. An agreed-upon way to check someone's whereabouts can give your family another verification tool during an emergency.

4) Pay attention when someone demands secrecy

Secrecy played a major role in Deborah's ordeal. The caller told her not to speak to anyone, listened during the transactions and gave her a fake explanation to use if someone asked questions. The FTC says urgency and secrecy are common characteristics of family emergency scams. If someone claims a loved one's survival depends on keeping you from contacting anyone else, treat that as a major warning.

5) Be extremely cautious about wire transfers

Scammers like payment methods that move money quickly and make recovery difficult. The FTC specifically warns about emergency scammers demanding wire transfers, cryptocurrency and gift cards.

If you've already sent money, contact the bank or transfer company immediately and ask whether it can stop or recall the transaction. Then report what happened to local police and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at https://t.co/Vq1B7cF2A8.

6) Reduce how much personal information criminals can find

Your name, relatives, phone numbers and other family connections can appear across people-search sites and data broker databases. That information can make a fake emergency more believable. I've tried manually removing my own information from these sites before, and keeping up with it can turn into a job because the information often returns.

A data removal service can help automate some of that work by requesting removal of your information from people-search sites and data broker databases. You can also learn more in our CyberGuy guide on removing your personal information from the web. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at https://t.co/ExMaVpavfo.

7) Talk about this scam before the phone rings

This may be the most useful conversation you have with your family this week. Tell them that a familiar voice can be faked. Agree that nobody sends emergency money until someone verifies the situation another way. A few minutes spent setting that expectation today could become extremely important when someone tries to scare you tomorrow.

Kurt's key takeaways

I've talked with a lot of scam victims over the years, and Deborah's story hit me hard. This wasn't some robotic impersonation that immediately made her suspicious. The voice sounded like her daughter having the kind of panic attack Deborah had heard before. For more than five hours, this guy kept her terrified and focused on one thing: getting Sarah home alive.

What stays with me most is where Deborah's mind went during that ordeal. Sitting in the car, she was already wondering how she would help Sarah recover from whatever these supposed kidnappers had done to her. That's a parent's mind at work. The money came later. Sarah came first.

I don't think the answer is expecting people to become experts at spotting fake audio. As the technology improves, a convincing voice could fool any of us. Instead, build another way to verify an emergency before one happens. Have a safe word, call your loved one directly and check with someone who may be physically near them. If your family feels comfortable using location sharing, set that up ahead of time.

Most importantly, talk about this with the people you love. Deborah had no idea this kind of voice scam was possible before that phone rang. Now she's sharing what happened because she doesn't want another parent sitting in a parking lot wondering whether their child is coming home. Watch or listen to my full conversation with Deborah on The CyberGuy Report podcast at https://t.co/ExMaVpavfo.
