Windows malware uses Grok AI to help stay hidden, researchers say https://t.co/ub2Vb7bDV6

A new piece of Windows malware is giving cybercriminals a lot of ways to cause trouble from one infected PC. It can steal passwords, grab browser cookies, route internet traffic through your computer and even burn through paid AI credits. Then there is the part that caught my attention. The malware, called x47.c, can reportedly use xAI's Grok to help decide how to keep itself running on an infected Windows computer.

Security researchers at Qrator Research Labs uncovered x47.c while tracking cybercrime activity. A threat actor using the name WraithTools has been advertising access to the malware, which comes with tools for stealing credentials and launching attacks. Qrator based its findings on the seller's advertisement, technical documentation, screenshots and follow-up messages, so the research shows what x47.c is advertised and designed to do rather than how widely it is currently infecting Windows PCs. Here's how it works, what the AI connection really means and the steps you can take to protect your Windows PC and accounts.

AI IS NOW POWERING CYBERATTACKS, MICROSOFT WARNS

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better health care.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare with AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed.

Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist.

Watch the free replays and get your checklists at https://t.co/x1SwswUebZ

How this Windows malware works

Once x47.c infects a Windows computer, the attacker can remotely control it through a management panel. Think of that infected PC as one computer in a larger network of machines controlled by the same criminal. Security researchers call that a botnet, but the important part for you is much simpler: someone else can potentially use your computer without your permission.

The operator can tell infected machines to launch online attacks. They can also steal information from those computers or use the victim's internet connection to route other traffic. Qrator found 18 advertised attack methods built into x47.c. Some can overwhelm websites and online services with traffic. Another targets something far newer: paid AI accounts.

Hackers can burn through paid AI credits

Many developers and businesses pay OpenAI, xAI and other AI companies based on how much they use their services. Access to those services often relies on a secret API key. You can think of that key as a password that lets an app communicate with an AI service and charge usage to an account.

If an attacker gets a valid API key, x47.c includes a feature that can repeatedly send requests to the AI provider. Those requests can use up prepaid credits or increase the victim's bill. Qrator describes this as a "Denial of Wallet" attack. The victim's website could keep working normally while the AI account behind part of it quietly chews through its available balance.

There is an important limit here. The attacker already needs a valid API key. x47.c does not magically break into an OpenAI or xAI account and create one. Still, that can become expensive quickly if an account allows automatic top-ups or high spending limits.

Grok can help the malware stay on your PC

The Grok connection sounds complicated, but the basic idea is pretty straightforward. Malware often tries to make sure it starts again after you reboot your computer. Security researchers call that persistence. x47.c includes what its seller calls an "AI Stealth" feature. According to Qrator, it can use Grok to look at the state of the infected computer and select from a predefined list of ways to maintain that access.

Those options include adding programs that run when Windows starts and creating scheduled tasks that can launch automatically. Grok does not appear to freely invent new attacks or control everything the malware does. Instead, it helps choose among options that the malware already has. The malware can also fall back on its own built-in methods if the AI request fails. So, cutting off its access to Grok would not necessarily remove the infection. We reached out to xAI for comment on the reported use of Grok and the safeguards it has in place to detect this kind of activity but did not hear back before our deadline.

Your saved passwords and browser sessions are targets

For most Windows users, this may be the most important part. x47.c advertises the ability to steal passwords saved in your browser. It can also collect browser cookies, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallet information and tokens tied to AI websites.

Browser cookies deserve special attention because some of them keep you signed in to websites. If malware steals an active login session, an attacker may be able to access an account without typing your password again. In some cases, changing the password alone may not immediately end a stolen session. That is why anyone dealing with an infected PC should also review active sessions and sign out of devices they do not recognize.

AI MALWARE CAN REWRITE ITSELF TO EVADE DETECTION

Your computer can also become someone else's internet connection

x47.c includes another feature called a SOCKS5 proxy. In plain English, that means a criminal can potentially route internet traffic through the infected computer. Online activity generated by the attacker could then appear to come from the victim's internet connection.

The malware's control panel lets operators see which infected computers are available to relay that traffic and whether those connections are still working. Meanwhile, the attacker can continue using the same infected machine to steal information or take part in online attacks.

9 ways to protect your Windows PC and accounts

You do not need to understand every technical feature inside x47.c to protect yourself. These steps can reduce your chances of getting infected and limit the damage if malware does reach your computer.

1) Keep Windows updated

Install Windows security updates promptly. Updates fix security weaknesses that attackers can use against PCs, even though Qrator has not identified a specific Windows vulnerability or infection method tied to x47.c. Go to Settings > Windows Update > Check for updates and install anything available.

Also remember that legitimate Windows updates come through Windows itself. A website that suddenly tells you to download a Windows update should make you suspicious. CyberGuy has previously covered fake Windows update pages that actually install malware.

2) Use strong security software

Keep strong antivirus or security software running and updated. Security tools can help catch malicious downloads and suspicious behavior before malware becomes deeply established on your computer. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at https://t.co/ExMaVpavfo.

3) Be careful about what you download

Avoid software from unfamiliar download sites, unexpected email links or pop-ups telling you that something needs an urgent update. Also be especially cautious if a webpage tells you to open Windows Run, PowerShell or Command Prompt and paste something into it. Cybercriminals increasingly use that trick to persuade people to install malware themselves. We recently covered thousands of hacked websites using fake verification prompts to push malicious Windows commands.

4) Use unique passwords

If malware steals one password, password reuse can turn one compromised account into several. Use a strong, unique password for every important account. A password manager can help create and store them.

5) Turn on two-factor authentication

Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) wherever possible. It gives attackers another obstacle if they obtain your password. However, remember that malware capable of stealing active browser sessions creates another risk, so 2FA should be one layer of your protection rather than your only one.

HALLUSQUATTING AI ATTACK COULD HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER

6) Sign out of active sessions after an infection

If you believe your PC has been infected, changing passwords should not be your only account step. From a separate trusted device, review active login sessions for your email, financial accounts, social accounts and other important services. Sign out of unfamiliar sessions or use the service's option to sign out everywhere. Also revoke authentication tokens or connected apps you no longer recognize. Qrator specifically warns that removing the malware does not undo credentials or tokens that attackers may have already stolen.

7) Protect your AI API keys

This one mainly applies to developers, businesses and anyone paying for AI through an API. Treat an API key like a password. Never publish it in a public code repository or leave it sitting in a document that other people can access. Review AI account usage and billing for requests you do not recognize. If you think a key has leaked, revoke it and create a new one. Also use spending limits, billing alerts and controls on automatic top-ups when your AI provider offers them. Those safeguards can limit how much an attacker could spend with a stolen key.

8) Disconnect the PC if you think it has been hacked

If your computer suddenly behaves strangely or you discover malware, disconnect it from the internet. Then open your trusted security software directly and run a full scan. Do not call phone numbers in pop-ups or follow instructions from unexpected warnings on your screen. Our CyberGuy guide on what to do if your computer has been hacked walks through the next steps.

9) Change sensitive passwords from another trusted device

If malware may have stolen information from your browser, use another clean device to change the passwords for your most important accounts. Start with your primary email account because password-reset messages for other services often go there. Then move to financial accounts and other sensitive services. After changing each password, review account activity and recovery information for anything you do not recognize.

Kurt's key takeaways

What gets my attention here isn't simply that the malware has the word AI attached to it. We've seen plenty of cyberthreats use AI as part of the sales pitch. What feels different with x47.c is how many jobs the attacker can handle from the same infected Windows PC. The malware can steal passwords and browser sessions, turn the computer into a traffic relay and help launch attacks. Then Grok can assist with choosing how the malware tries to keep its foothold on that machine. Still, the most useful lesson for you comes back to the security basics. One of many prohibitively priced “premium” products available from the channel’s perpetually promoted Online Merch Store…

Not long after, came an explosive hit piece, “ignited” by an ill-fated representative in LTT’s testing department, who dared to imply GN’s benchmark data had been accrued from “recycled results”.  GN countered by surgically analysing Linus’s own “superficial” reviews and unearthed such inconsistencies as, inexplicably favourable recommendations for Noctua’s CPU coolers, despite their performing worse than cheaper alternatives such Thermalright’s “Peerless Assassin”…or delivering results under maximum workloads that would’ve been impossible by virtue of their cooled CPU’s higher idle temperatures.  

Further damaging errata, included misquoting specs on the packaging of a certain manufacturers “combustible” power supplies, neglecting to remove the protective cellophane on the underside of a novelty mouse…thereby impeding its  optical sensor’s tracking ability…and…perhaps best of all…installing GPU coolers back to front down.

text:
Oregon's affordable housing industrial complex is awash in billions in taxpayer money, federal tax credits, private investors...as well as serious questions surrounding lack of accountability and corruption.

And now the person who overseas the lion's share of that system (Oregon Housing and Community Services - or OHCS), is facing a serious ethics review.

OHCS executive director, Andrea Bell, failed to disclose her husband's employment with JH Brawner, a consulting firm involved in the multiple affordable housing projects that received 10's of millions of dollars from her agency.

Bell only amended her financial disclosures once reporters began asking her questions.

But there's an even bigger story here:

OHSC has distributed more than $1.4 billion in state housing subsidies over five years. That doesn't include the enormous value of federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC) allocated through the agency.

Here's how LIHTC works: Developers receive allocations of federal tax credits, which are then sold to private investors in exchange for capital. Investors then receive federal tax benefits over ten years, while developers receive financing for projects.

It's an incredibly complex system that brings together government agencies (such as OHCS), private developers (such as Community Development Partners - or CDP), banks and financial institutions, and large investment firms. And the public deserves to know exactly where the money goes.

Nearly two years ago, we investigated Milepost 5, a Portland affordable housing complex that had descended into deplorable conditions (as affordable housing properties tend to do) despite millions in public subsidies and tax-credit financing.

Our investigation revealed that the investment entity CDP, a private California company that develops many affordable housing projects in the Portland-metro area, is a subsidiary of Aegon Group, an international hedge fund worth north of $300 billion.

Although OHCS awarded CDP $3.3 million for upgrades and repairs at Milepost 5, serious maintenance problems persisted, along with drug dealing, squatters, and repeated complaints from residents and neighbors. At one point, there was even a raid by Homeland Security Investigations at the property, in which they arrested multiple drug dealers who had taken up residence in the building.

CDP claimed that seismic upgrades consumed most of the $3.3 million, despite an earlier estimate of approximately $350,000 for the seismic work. According to CDP, this left insufficient funding to address many of the property's other problems.

After contacting multiple people within CDP, OHCS, and local government, we were unable to obtain a satisfactory accounting of exactly how the $3.3 million was spent. Everyone involved just wanted the questions about the funds to go away.

In fact, a local whistleblower who lives near Milepost 5 was threatened with arrest after U.S. Senator Jeff Merkley’s office allegedly identified him as a man who had been behaving threateningly outside the senator’s office. There was just one problem: the whistleblower was out of town on a fishing trip at the time, and the man in question bore no resemblance to him. Nevertheless, the accusation reportedly led to an attempt to have the whistleblower arrested. Even after the mistaken identity was established, neither Merkley nor his office offered the whistleblower an apology. Senator Merkley needs to answer to this egregious behavior. 

While OHCS did publicly admonish CDP for its failures at Milepost 5 at a meeting, two weeks later, the agency approved $43.6 million to CDP for the Julia West affordable housing project. 

In a news story by ProPublica (see below) the publication exposed how Oregon law shields detailed financial information about subsidized housing developments from public scrutiny. 

There are billions in state subsidies. Federal tax credits benefitting private investors. Complex ownership structures. Limited public access to financial records.

And now an ethics review involving the director of the agency responsible for overseeing much of it.

Both the Bell controversy and Milepost 5 raise fundamental questions about oversight, transparency, and whose interests Oregon's affordable housing system is actually serving. 

Because it doesn't seem to serve the people who are unfortunate enough to have to live in places like Milepost 5 or any of the other dozens of affordable housing projects in this city that are constantly falling into disrepair. It seems to mostly serve out of state corporations and huge international hedge funds.

The state (i.e. Gov. Kotek) and local government tell us that affordable housing should be about providing safe, stable homes for the people who really need them - not for moving enormous sums of public money through an increasingly complicated financial industrial complex, one that appears to be rife with corruption.

Below are the articles from ProPublica and our article about Milepost 5.

Buchanan gave South Carolina an informal pledge to preserve the status quo in Charleston Harbor and not move troops from Fort Moultrie. Floyd, who had favored a hands-off policy, resigned, saying the distrust could only lead to war, as Federal assurances were now meaningless.

The pattern continued under Lincoln. Governor Pickens granted Gustavus Fox access to Sumter after Fox assured him the visit was for peaceful purposes connected to possible abandonment; Fox returned with a detailed assessment of the garrison’s supplies and the feasibility of a night relief. Ward Hill Lamon, Lincoln’s personal friend and special agent, was likewise allowed to meet Anderson and Pickens under diplomatic cover and left both with the clear impression that evacuation was imminent. Lincoln himself was reported to have told William Cabell Rives that if Virginia stayed in the Union he would abandon Sumter—an offer later echoed in talks with Virginia convention delegates. Seward spent weeks privately signaling Confederate commissioners that the fort would be given up, while Alexander Stephens publicly stated on March 21 in his so-called "Cornerstone Speech" that Sumter would soon be abandoned.  

No record shows Lincoln was unaware of Seward’s contacts, and the cumulative effect of these conflicting assurances left Governor Pickens with no reliable way to judge whether the April notice of “provisions only” meant food or the opening of a reinforcement effort. Teapot

茶壶——美国波士顿1740年左右

这件茶壶由18世纪美国银匠雅各布·赫德（Jacob Hurd，1702–1758）打造，是马萨诸塞州波士顿手工银器的代表作之一。整体尺寸为高14.8厘米，长22.6厘米（含把手），仅壶身高12.6厘米。茶壶采用纯银制成，展现了当时波士顿银匠精湛的锻造技巧和对细节的严格把控。

银质表面光洁，形态稳重而优雅，造型设计典雅实用。壶顶配有一个宝珠状的钮，但据记录该钮可能不是原配，后期更换的可能性较大。细观壶身，铭刻有惠普尔（Whipple）家族的纹章，强调了身份和所有权，这种刻章不仅是装饰手法，也是当时工艺品归属的权威标识。

茶壶的制作时期正值18世纪中叶，恰逢新兴的美洲殖民地社会逐渐形成独特的文化身份，银器不仅作为日用器皿，也体现了主人的社会地位和身份认同。雅各布·赫德是当时波士顿著名银匠，这只茶壶也因此承载了丰富的历史背景和工艺传统。

观赏时应注意壶体的比例和线条流畅度，银器的光泽和雕刻细节，尤其是徽章部分的精细雕琢。此外，壶钮的非原装状态提醒我们关注文物的保护和时代更迭给物品带来的变化。

此茶壶由J. H. Wade赠予博物馆，曾为Lawrence Park所有，收藏历史为其增添了展品的文化价值。总体而言，通过这件银器，我们得以窥见18世纪美国殖民地社会的生活气息及工匠的匠心独运，展现了一段历史与艺术交织的篇章。

Teapot circa 1740, Boston, Massachusetts

This silver teapot was crafted around 1740 by Jacob Hurd (1702–1758), a prominent American silversmith based in Boston, Massachusetts. Measuring 14.8 cm in height and 22.6 cm in length including the handle, with the body alone at 12.6 cm tall, it exemplifies mid-18th-century colonial American silverwork. The teapot is made entirely of silver, reflecting the refined techniques and careful workmanship characteristic of Hurd's studio.

The piece exhibits a balanced and elegant form, maintaining both aesthetic refinement and practical design. Notably, the finial atop the lid is likely a later addition and not original to the teapot, which speaks to the historical process of alteration and preservation in such objects. Engraved on the body is the coat of arms of the Whipple family, a clear marker of identity and ownership. This heraldic engraving functions both as decorative art and as an authoritative signifier of provenance, common in silverware of the period.

The teapot dates from a formative period in American colonial society when objects like silverware symbolized more than utilitarian use: they communicated social status and personal identity within the community. Jacob Hurd was a well-known Boston silversmith, and pieces from his hand often carry significant cultural and historical weight. This teapot, with its precise construction and detailed embellishment, offers insight into the material culture and craftsmanship of the time.

When examining the teapot, attention should be given to the overall proportions and smooth flow of its lines, the reflective surface of the silver, and particularly to the finely executed coat of arms engraving. The non-original finial invites contemplation of the object's changing history and the impact of conservation decisions.

The teapot entered the museum collection as a gift from J. H. Wade and was previously owned by Lawrence Park, adding layers to its documented ownership history. Through this single piece, viewers gain a tangible connection to 18th-century colonial life and the artisanal skill embodied in early American decorative arts, underscoring the intertwined narrative of identity, craftsmanship, and historical context.

FRIDAY, OCTOBER 9, 2026

THE PEOPLE, PROJECTS & IDEAS SHAPING WHAT'S NEXT

This week, El Salvador's publicly reported Bitcoin treasury crossed another milestone, a collaboration between the Bitcoin Office and the Ministry of Agriculture brought Texas cattle genetics to the country, and Salvadoran students explored the technologies behind Bitcoin and artificial intelligence.

Meanwhile, a Salvadoran robotics researcher received recognition for his scientific publication record, and El Salvador's AI strategy reached an international audience in San Francisco.

From Bitcoin reserves to cattle breeding, from computer science to robotics, this week's developments illustrate the range of projects taking shape across El Salvador.

🇸🇻₿ 1. EL SALVADOR'S BITCOIN TREASURY CROSSES 7,800 BTC

A NEW MILESTONE FOR THE NATIONAL BITCOIN RESERVE

El Salvador's publicly reported Bitcoin holdings reached a new milestone on Friday, October 9.

According to a screenshot of the National Bitcoin Office's official treasury dashboard circulated by Bitcoin Magazine and reposted by the Bitcoin Office, the country's holdings reached approximately 7,800.37 BTC.

The milestone follows the 7,792.37 BTC balance recorded in our previous weekly report on October 2.

That represents an increase of approximately eight Bitcoin in seven days.

The dashboard's balance-history chart continues to show a rising treasury balance, a development that has attracted attention from international Bitcoin publications.

The Bitcoin Office also reposted commentary celebrating El Salvador's continued Bitcoin accumulation.

The latest figures offer another chapter in a national Bitcoin story that began with the country's adoption of Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021 and continues to attract international attention.

7,800 BTC AND COUNTING. 🇸🇻₿

🐂₿ 2. FROM TEXAS TO EL SALVADOR: THE ARRIVAL OF BITCOIN BEEFSTEAK

BITCOIN OFFICE AND MAG COLLABORATE ON LIVESTOCK GENETICS

One of the week's most unexpected Bitcoin-related stories came from El Salvador's agricultural sector.

The Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MAG), working with the National Bitcoin Office, announced the addition of two Santa Gertrudis breeding bulls to support efforts to improve the country's cattle genetics.

One of the animals was imported from Texas, United States.

Vice Minister of Agriculture and Livestock Óscar Domínguez explained that the breeding program is intended to improve the genetic quality of Salvadoran cattle herds.

“These bulls are and will be the fathers of thousands of calves throughout the country,” Domínguez stated.

The broader MAG reproductive program includes several cattle breeds, among them Senepol, Brown Swiss, Girolando, Brahman and Angus.

The ministry also offers semen doses to livestock producers starting at $2.83, making genetic improvement services available through its animal reproduction facilities.

A WELCOME AT THE AIRPORT

Bitcoin Office Director Stacy Herbert shared photographs of the arrival of the Santa Gertrudis bulls from Texas.

The images showed a group welcoming the animals at the airport, including Herbert and Max Keiser.

The Bitcoin Office celebrated the initiative with a distinctly Bitcoin-flavored message:

“Better genetics, better beef.”

And then came the line that gave the story its name:

“The era of Bitcoin Beefsteak has arrived.”

The collaboration highlights the Bitcoin Office's participation in an initiative beyond the digital-asset sector, connecting its international network with a practical agricultural development project.

For Salvadoran cattle producers, the objective is straightforward: better genetics and improved breeding opportunities.

FROM TEXAS RANCHES TO SALVADORAN FARMS. 🇸🇻🐂

₿🎓 3. CUBO+ TAKES STUDENTS DOWN THE BITCOIN RABBIT HOLE

TOM TABER EXPLORES THE TECHNOLOGY AND IDEAS BEHIND BITCOIN

On October 8, Bitcoin educator and Montaña Sagrada co-founder Tom Taber delivered a special class to CUBO+ students in San Salvador.

The session, titled “Bitcoin Rabbit Holes,” explored aspects of Bitcoin extending beyond its market price.

According to CUBO+, the discussion examined Bitcoin's technological foundations, its influence on society and its potential implications for El Salvador's future.

Photographs from the classroom showed students working on laptops while Taber discussed topics including monetary systems, computer science, cryptography and game theory.

Before the session, Taber described the opportunity to speak with Salvadoran students as a privilege.

He praised the country's Bitcoin community and expressed enthusiasm about sharing his knowledge with students he described as future leaders.

CUBO+ subsequently confirmed that the class had taken place, publishing photographs of the session and thanking Taber for his participation.

The class illustrates an important part of El Salvador's Bitcoin education ecosystem: exposure to experienced international educators and the opportunity to examine the technology from multiple disciplines.

BEYOND THE PRICE. BEHIND THE PROTOCOL. INTO THE FUTURE. ₿

🤖💻 4. FROM MACHINE LEARNING TO AI AGENTS: CUBO AI STUDENTS BUILD WHAT COMES NEXT

TWO HANDS-ON LEARNING EXPERIENCES IN ONE WEEK

El Salvador's AI education ecosystem continued moving forward this week as CUBO AI students participated in practical sessions covering machine learning fundamentals and AI-powered workflows.

OCTOBER 4 — UNDERSTANDING HOW MACHINES LEARN

Instructor Camila Cruz, working with CUBO AI and C2 Labs AI, led a class focused on machine learning from first principles.

Students explored mathematical foundations, built basic algorithms, trained a model and observed it generating predictions.

The session also introduced the perceptron, a foundational building block of neural networks.

By examining weights, biases and activation functions, participants explored how mathematical operations help machine-learning models process information.

The emphasis was on understanding the technology rather than simply using ready-made AI tools.

OCTOBER 9 — PUTTING AI AGENTS TO WORK

On Friday, CUBO AI continued its hands-on training with a workshop focused on Fluso, an AI workspace designed to support automated workflows.

Instructors Moisés Iglesias and Rodrigo Trujillo guided students through the platform, examining how AI agents can assist with practical tasks.

According to CUBO AI's posts, participants compared Fluso's features with other AI tools before working directly with the platform.

The two sessions illustrated complementary skills: understanding how machine learning operates and learning how AI-powered systems can be applied to real workflows.

For Salvadoran students preparing to enter a technology-driven economy, both are relevant areas of technical education.

FIRST, LEARN HOW AI WORKS. THEN, LEARN HOW TO BUILD WITH IT. 🇸🇻🤖

🏆🤖 5. ANIA HIGHLIGHTS SALVADORAN ROBOTICS RESEARCHER'S SCIENTIFIC MILESTONE

DR. MANUEL CARDONA RECORDS 141 SCOPUS-INDEXED PUBLICATIONS

El Salvador's National Artificial Intelligence Agency (ANIA) recognized a scientific publication milestone involving one of its strategic advisers.

On October 6, ANIA congratulated Dr. Manuel Cardona after he appeared first in a ranking of ten Salvadoran researchers by number of Scopus-indexed publications.

According to the ranking shared by Cardona, using figures dated September 30, 2026, the researcher had accumulated 141 indexed publications.

The ten researchers included in the ranking accounted for a combined 449 publications.

Cardona, affiliated with STEAM Robotics Academy, represented approximately 31.4% of that total.

His research includes kinematics, mechatronics and autonomous systems—disciplines closely connected to robotics and the emerging field of physical AI.

THE RESEARCH ECOSYSTEM BEHIND THE NUMBERS

The ranking also highlighted the contribution of Salvadoran universities.

The University of El Salvador placed six researchers among the ten listed, accounting for 221 publications.

The Technological University of El Salvador contributed two researchers, while the Central American University José Simeón Cañas had one.

Cardona's position drew attention to STEAM Robotics Academy's growing involvement in scientific research alongside its educational activities.

The ranking measures publication volume, rather than research quality or impact, but it provides a useful snapshot of scientific activity across Salvadoran institutions.

For ANIA, the recognition also highlights the research experience represented within its advisory network.

141 PUBLICATIONS. ROBOTICS. AUTONOMOUS SYSTEMS. SALVADORAN SCIENTIFIC TALENT. 🇸🇻🔬

🌎🤖 6. EL SALVADOR'S AI STRATEGY REACHES SAN FRANCISCO TECH WEEK

GINGER LUCKEY GAETZ PRESENTS EL SALVADOR'S APPROACH TO EMERGING TECHNOLOGY

The agency emphasized its preference for innovation-friendly frameworks and opportunities for emerging technologies.

Gaetz's participation connected El Salvador's national AI ambitions with a broader international discussion involving technology founders, investors and industry specialists.

The appearance complements the country's domestic AI education initiatives, bringing international engagement and local talent development into the same weekly picture.

@grok Build updated to 1.0.51

Breaking Changes:

• Cancel and edit-resend on long sessions no longer unexpectedly revert workspace files

• Inline viewports can now be restored at a previously saved screen area without extra cursor queries

• New /density command and Tool call density setting let you choose how much detail tool calls show in the transcript

• Web fetch approval cards now include "always allow" and "never allow" domain options that persist for the folder

• Slash command completion now updates live when skills are added or changed during a session

• Chrome profiles can now be persisted across restarts using durable state directories

• Workspace server sessions now share one Chrome instance for cookies and storage

• /feedback Drafts tab now supports G / Home and End to jump to the first or last draft

• Pinned sessions on the dashboard now stay in the order you pinned or reordered them

• Shift+Enter, Ctrl+., Ctrl+/ and Ctrl+[ / ] now work inside tmux when extended-keys are enabled

• grok -p --output-format json now reports the exact worktree folder used (useful after -w name collisions)

• Bare hook commands such as my-guard now run from PATH when not found next to the hook file

• Headless JSON error output now includes the worktree folder when a session was started

• grok sessions list and /resume now show worktree sessions started from the same subfolder

• /exit (and aliases) in a dashboard details view now closes only that session instead of quitting Grok

• Editors offering file access now receive a one-time transcript notice that the agent reads and writes disk files

• config.toml now accepts an [update] section without breaking other commands

• grok worktree commands now work correctly inside Jujutsu repositories

• Images pasted with skill commands like /pr-workflow are now sent to the model

• Invalid model provider tables now produce a clear startup error instead of silent fallback

• Narrow feedback dialog now shows full draft titles and readable confirm prompts

• /workflow stop|resume <name> now correctly targets the live run instead of an ended first run

• Dialogs like /feedback no longer disappear on very short terminal windows

• Delete operations now respect the same permission rules as shell rm commands

• Hooks can no longer rewrite a web-search call to restrict domains

• Workspace server now starts with per-session private Chrome by default

• Notification hooks for permission prompts and task completion now run reliably before a headless session exits

• Headless goal runs no longer print a spurious "Goal paused" message after completion

• Legacy UI density settings now combine correctly across config tiers and produce expected folding

• Approval answers sent after a turn ends no longer affect the turn

• Background shell commands now fail immediately when the working directory does not exist

• grok worktree rm without -f now safely keeps worktrees when the unsaved-work check fails or times out

• The dashboard slash menu now shows skills from the home session even when opened early

• grok worktree rm and gc now correctly remove worktrees whose only untracked content is empty folders

• Editing a queued prompt now prevents accidental removal with a stale client view

• The model is now told when memory is turned off or on for the session

• Hook results in the UI now correctly distinguish between notes and tool outcomes

• Permission cards for MCP tools can no longer be tricked into showing fake option rows

• The agent stdio mode now returns clearer errors for malformed client requests and consistent recap replies

• Scroll logging and acceleration calculations no longer produce backwards timestamps under load

• Hooks and tool commands started from the TUI can no longer read or write the interactive terminal

• Delete operations now correctly match Bash(rm ...) ask/deny rules even when the path contains .. or the cwd is a symlink

• With goals disabled, a headless /goal line is now treated as a normal prompt instead of failing

• Only slash commands at the start of a message trigger skills

• disable_zdr_incompatible_tools changes now apply to new turns without restarting the worker

• Project skills are now labeled correctly for nested projects

Performance:

• Opening the resume picker is now much faster on machines with many worktrees

• grok worktree commands start faster by skipping unnecessary model catalog work at boot
